strengths: The proposed framework addresses a core challenge in task and motion planning (TAMP): eliminating the labor-intensive manual construction of PDDL planning domains and manual motion-constraint mapping.
The combination of physical simulation to verify geometric/physical feasibility with LLMs to hypothesize semantic predicates and PDDL actions is conceptually sensible and effective.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 diverse task domains and 1,200 evaluation problems, demonstrating high planning success rates and strong generalization to scenarios with larger numbers of objects.
Good comparison with advanced reasoning models (o1 and R1), illustrating the time and token efficiency advantages of deriving a modular domain offline versus prompting LLMs to plan online.
Validation on three physical robot platforms (Agilex Piper, Franka Emika Panda, UR5e) as well as integration with both classical motion planners and a learned VLA policy.
weaknesses: The evaluation compares exclusively against LLM-as-planner baselines (such as LLMTAMP variants and RuleAsMem) rather than existing domain induction or predicate learning methods (e.g., Silver et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2024). Even if those methods have different input assumptions, benchmarking against or thoroughly comparing domain generation quality with them would provide stronger context.

The system relies on predefined continuous feature spaces (Cartesian coordinates, bounding boxes/sizes, RGB values) and simple grid-like interval partitioning. The sensitivity of the method to the grid resolution parameter $u$ and its scalability to higher-dimensional continuous interactions are not deeply analyzed.

The title claims 'A Single Demonstration', but compositional and multi-step tasks (e.g., bridge building, rearrangement) require multiple demonstrations of different primitive sub-tasks (e.g., pick, stack, align) to construct the complete domain.

strengths: Addresses a core bottleneck in Task and Motion Planning (TAMP): eliminating the need for manually engineered PDDL domains and handcrafted symbolic-to-geometric bindings.
A well-grounded neuro-symbolic design: combining physical simulation roll-outs to establish physically valid continuous boundaries with LLM reasoning to invent interpretable predicates and actions.

The Logical Constraint Adapter (LoCA) effectively bridges high-level symbolic plans to low-level motion planning by converting predicate boundaries into constrained motion planning inequalities without manual operator engineering.

Thorough empirical evaluation across 9 environments and over 1,200 tasks, including scalability tests up to 20 objects, comparison with modern reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1), and hardware deployment across three physical robot platforms (Agilex Piper, Franka Panda, and UR5e with a π0 VLA policy).
weaknesses: The continuous feature space discretization (axis-aligned interval partitioning) is relatively simple and may face combinatorial explosion or expressivity issues in higher-dimensional geometric interactions (e.g., full SE(3) pose reasoning, non-convex shapes, continuous contact manifolds, or articulated mechanisms).

High dependence on precise continuous state perception (e.g., object poses, CAD models, bounding intervals) and simulation fidelity during the predicate imagination phase, which limits immediate applicability to raw perceptual inputs or unstructured scenes.

The claim 'one demonstration is all it takes' is slightly overstated: compositional and multi-stage tasks (e.g., bridge building, rearrangement) require multiple demonstrations covering individual sub-skills (pick, align, stack) to compose the domain, as unobserved actions or latent constraints cannot be induced from an incomplete single demonstration.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and well-known challenge in Task and Motion Planning (TAMP): eliminating the labor-intensive requirement of manually engineering symbolic planning domains and their geometric constraints.

The proposed framework (PDDLLM) introduces a creative pipeline that couples physical simulation roll-outs with LLM reasoning to invent both first-order/higher-order predicates and logical actions from minimal demonstrations.

The Logical Constraint Adapter (LoCA) provides an automated bridge from symbolic action effects back into constrained motion planning queries, removing the need for manually coded logic-geometric programming bindings.

Extensive experimental evaluation across nine diverse task domains, with comprehensive baselines (including frontier reasoning models like OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1, failure-feedback loops, and memory ablations) and analysis across scaling object counts and time limits.

Physical robot deployment across three distinct manipulator platforms (Franka Panda, Agilex Piper, UR5e), including successful validation demonstrating compatibility with a vision-language-action (VLA) policy (pi-0).
weaknesses: The claim of generating domains 'without manual predesign' is somewhat overstated; the methodology relies on a pre-specified feature space (e.g., Cartesian coordinates, RGB colors, dimensions) and predefined feature partitioning hyperparameters ($u$). This shifts manual engineering effort from writing PDDL to engineering feature spaces, interval boundaries, and prompting templates.

The predicate imagination technique relies on grid-like subspace partitioning and sampling in PyBullet. While this works well for simple axis-aligned geometric relationships (e.g., on top, beside, aligned), it may suffer from the curse of dimensionality or fail to capture complex non-linear geometric configurations (such as continuous 3D orientations in SO(3), articulated mechanics, or non-rigid contact dynamics).

LoCA assumes action effects can be mapped directly to static mathematical inequality constraints on object features for an off-the-shelf motion planner. This formulation is well-suited for pick-and-place style tasks, but it is unclear how it extends to complex, continuous dynamic interactions (e.g., pouring, wiping, or compliant insertions).

The reliance on full, noise-free continuous state information (via CAD models and ArUco markers) bypasses raw visual perception challenges, leaving the system sensitive to perception inaccuracies and segmentation ambiguities in unstructured real-world environments.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) by automating the derivation of symbolic predicates and action definitions from single demonstrations rather than relying on human engineering or large curated datasets.
The synergy between physics simulation (for ground-truth feasibility filtering) and LLMs (for symbolic abstraction and semantic reasoning) is well-designed and conceptually sound.

The Logical Constraint Adapter (LoCA) effectively bridges symbolic action effects with continuous motion planners by extracting geometric inequality constraints, avoiding the need for pre-programmed skill primitives.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 9 distinct environments and over 1,200 planning tasks, showing substantial performance gains over both standard LLM-planners and strong reasoning models (o1, R1).
Solid real-robot validation across three different manipulator arms (Franka Panda, Agilex Piper, and UR5e) as well as successful integration with a learned vision-language-action policy (Pi0).
weaknesses: The method still relies on an engineered feature space representation (e.g., explicit 3D positions, orientations, dimensions, and colors obtained via CAD models or ArUco markers), which weakens the claim of learning domains entirely 'from scratch'.

Predicate imagination relies on running thousands of parallel simulation roll-outs over uniformly sampled continuous states; this restricts applicability to environments where an accurate simulator with object assets is readily available.

Feature space discretization via interval slicing can face curse-of-dimensionality challenges in scenarios requiring complex articulated or contact-rich interactions beyond basic relative spatial thresholds.
Minor clarity and naming discrepancies in the appendix (e.g., referring to unreleased 'Qwen3' backbones in Table 19 instead of Qwen2/Qwen2.5).

strengths: The ambition to synthesize complete, executable PDDL domains from demonstration trajectories and natural language instructions with minimal human intervention is important and timely for task and motion planning (TAMP).

The paper includes extensive evaluations spanning nine simulation environments, 1,200 evaluation tasks, and physical hardware experiments on three robot platforms (Franka Panda, Agilex Piper, and UR5e).

The paper is clearly structured and accompanied by thorough appendix sections documenting prompt templates, sensitivity analyses (e.g., on discretization resolution u and prompt count), and real-robot setup details.
weaknesses: Fundamentally mismatched baseline comparison: The paper claims superiority over prior methods, yet it compares PDDLLM (which uses derived PDDL domains solved by a classical symbolic PDDL solver) exclusively against pure LLM-based task planners (LLMTAMP, o1-TAMP, R1-TAMP) generating text-based action sequences directly. It is well-established that pure LLM autoregressive generation struggles with long combinatorial horizons (e.g., Tower of Hanoi), whereas classical PDDL solvers excel. To genuinely evaluate the quality of domain induction, the paper must compare against established domain and predicate learning baselines (e.g., Silver et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2024; Wong et al., 2023).

Heavy reliance on rigid scaffolding and heuristics: While presented as automated derivation from scratch, the system relies on strong assumptions: manually specified continuous feature spaces (positions, colors, sizes), uniform sampling and axis-aligned interval partitioning, and rigid prompt templates. The LLM predominantly performs syntactic translation and naming for pre-computed interval differences and state transitions rather than autonomous conceptual induction.

Limitations of the Logical Constraint Adapter (LoCA): LoCA treats predicate effects as simple axis-aligned box/interval inequalities passed to a motion planner. While this works for simple tabletop pick-and-place, alignment, and stacking, it does not generalize to realistic 6-DoF manipulation involving non-trivial contact dynamics, kinematic reachability, complex geometry, or non-prehensile skills.

Overstated single-demonstration capability: Learning robust action preconditions from a single demonstration trajectory is inherently under-constrained. As acknowledged in the appendix, the system frequently misses complex composite preconditions (e.g., ordering constraints), requiring either trial-and-error backtracking in planning or multi-demonstration curation (Table 4).

strengths: Addresses an important and longstanding bottleneck in task and motion planning (TAMP): eliminating the heavy human engineering required to specify PDDL domains, actions, and predicates.

The proposed PDDLLM framework effectively integrates LLMs with physical simulation validation to derive grounded first-order predicates and discrete action transitions from a single continuous demonstration.
The Logical Constraint Adapter (LoCA) provides an automated bridge from symbolic action effects directly into constrained motion planning queries without manually written operator samplers.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering 1,200 task instances across 9 domains, spanning long horizons (up to 510 steps) and scaling up to 20 objects.
Extensive hardware experiments demonstrating successful real-robot execution on three distinct robot manipulators (Piper, Franka Panda, UR5e), including integration with a learned VLA policy (pi0).
Thorough appendix providing extensive ablations on hyperparameter sensitivity (discretization scale u), prompt variations, LLM backbones, and parallel sampling budgets.
weaknesses: Missing comparisons with dedicated domain/predicate learning baselines: The evaluation primarily compares against LLM-based prompt planners (LLMTAMP, o1-TAMP, R1-TAMP, RuleAsMem). Because PDDLLM executes plans using an off-the-shelf symbolic planner (PDDLStream), comparing it against LLM generation baselines heavily biases results in favor of PDDLLM. Comparing against existing domain induction methods (e.g., Predicators / Silver et al. 2023, Kumar et al. 2023, or APDI / Huang et al. 2025) would be much more informative.

Strong assumptions on feature space and state representations: The system assumes continuous features (Cartesian poses, RGB values, bounding dimensions) and object CAD/URDF models are already known and structured. Discretizing these into axis-aligned interval bounds relies on hand-crafted scene description templates and conservative heuristics (dmin), limiting applicability to complex non-rigid dynamics or freeform continuous geometric constraints.

Simplistic formulation of motion constraints in LoCA: LoCA maps predicate physical constraints represented as axis-aligned box inequalities to motion planners. Many realistic TAMP manipulation skills require non-trivial SE(3) end-effector orientations, non-convex collision checks, approach directions, and grasp samplers that cannot be expressed purely through interval bounds.

High upfront token cost and dependency on parallel generation: A single generation run has a 41.7% failure rate (Table 15), necessitating 10-20 parallel prompts and extensive simulation roll-outs (~300k-550k tokens per domain) to filter valid domains.

Minor presentation errors: In Table 6, the header mistakenly repeats 'o1-TAMP' twice instead of labeling the third column 'R1-TAMP'; 'Tower of Hanoi' is inconsistently spelled as 'Tower of Hannoi' throughout the text and figures.
